animals.behavior_notes: California Red-legged Frogs breed in late winter during California's rainy season when pond levels are highest, with males calling from dense emergent vegetation to attract females. This federally threatened species has declined dramatically due to habitat loss, introduced bullfrogs, and disease.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit freshwater ponds, marshes, and slow streams within Point Reyes or other protected coastal areas after winter rains; listen for their low, guttural, stuttering call. Binoculars are helpful as they often remain hidden in dense cattails and rushes — avoid approaching too close as they are easily disturbed.

animals.name: Wood Frog
animals.behavior_notes: Wood Frogs are among the first amphibians to breed each spring, often calling from vernal pools while snow still lingers on the ground, with males producing a distinctive duck-like quacking chorus. They are freeze-tolerant, surviving winter with ice crystals forming within their bodies.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit forested vernal pools on the first warm rains of late winter when nighttime temperatures exceed 40°F — the explosive breeding aggregation typically lasts only a few days and is easy to miss. Listen for the communal quacking chorus audible from a considerable distance, then approach the pool's edge quietly.

animals.name: American Toad
animals.behavior_notes: American Toads breed in spring when males produce a long, melodious trill from shallow ponds and puddles that can last 30 seconds or more, creating a chorus audible from great distances. After breeding they disperse widely into gardens, forests, and fields where they hunt insects and earthworms at night.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit any shallow pond or roadside puddle on warm spring nights and listen for the sustained musical trill; males are highly visible and approach closely without fleeing. In summer, look under porch lights and in gardens at dusk where toads gather to hunt insects attracted to artificial lighting.

animals.name: Spotted Salamander
animals.behavior_notes: Spotted Salamanders undertake dramatic mass migrations to vernal pools on the first warm (above 40°F), rainy nights of late winter, sometimes crossing roads in the hundreds to reach ancestral breeding pools. After depositing their distinctive egg masses — which contain symbiotic green algae — adults return underground and are rarely seen again until the following year.
animals.viewing_tips: On the first warm rainy night of late winter, drive slowly on wooded rural roads near forested wetlands and scan with a flashlight for these boldly spotted black-and-yellow salamanders crossing pavement. Arrive at known vernal pools just after dark during rain events for the best chance of witnessing a full migration event.

animals.name: Axolotl
parks: Xochimilco Ecological Park (no established US NP population)
animals.behavior_notes: Axolotls are critically endangered and native to Lake Xochimilco in Mexico. They are neotenic, retaining larval features throughout their lives, and are most active in cooler, calm waters.
animals.viewing_tips: Axolotls do not exist in the wild in the United States and are effectively extinct in their native Mexican habitat. Your best chance of seeing one is at a zoo or aquarium such as the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago or the Denver Zoo.

animals.name: Spring Peeper
animals.behavior_notes: Spring Peepers emerge from winter dormancy as early as late February and are among the first signs of spring. Males gather in large choruses near ponds and wetlands, producing their iconic high-pitched peeping calls to attract mates.
animals.viewing_tips: Listen for their loud, shrill peeping calls near shallow wetlands, ponds, and flooded meadows after dusk on mild evenings. Approach slowly with a red-filtered flashlight — they will go silent when disturbed, so patience and stillness are key to spotting them.

animals.name: Atlantic Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Atlantic Salmon return to coastal Maine rivers in fall to spawn, making upstream runs visible in shallow riffles and pools. Their leaping behavior at falls and rapids makes them detectable even from shore.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit the Narraguagus or Machias Rivers near Acadia in October for the best chance of seeing spawning runs. Look for fish jumping at natural barriers or resting in calm pools.

animals.name: Chinook Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Chinook Salmon make their spawning runs up the Hoh, Queets, and Quinault Rivers in fall, gathering in large numbers in gravel-bottomed shallows. Their large size — often exceeding 30 pounds — makes them easy to spot when present.
animals.viewing_tips: The Hoh River corridor in Olympic National Park offers accessible bank viewing during peak spawning. Polarized sunglasses dramatically improve visibility into the water.

animals.name: Sockeye Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Sockeye Salmon turn brilliant red during their spawning run and pack Brooks River in Katmai in staggering numbers during summer. They congregate below Brooks Falls where bears famously gather to intercept them.
animals.viewing_tips: Reserve a spot on the Brooks Falls viewing platform well in advance — demand is extremely high in July. The fish are most densely packed and visible mid-morning through afternoon.

animals.name: Coho Salmon
animals.behavior_notes: Coho Salmon enter Olympic Peninsula rivers in mid-to-late fall, spawning in smaller tributary streams and secondary channels. Their bright red and green coloration makes them visually distinctive in clear water.
animals.viewing_tips: Check smaller feeder creeks off the Hoh and Sol Duc Rivers where Coho often spawn away from crowds. Low-angle morning light helps reduce surface glare for better fish visibility.

animals.name: Steelhead Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Steelhead Trout make winter spawning runs into coastal California rivers, entering freshwater after heavy rains raise river levels. They hold in deep pools and runs between spawning bouts.
animals.viewing_tips: The Smith and Redwood Creek watersheds within Redwood National Park offer accessible winter steelhead viewing from bridges and riverbanks. Visit after significant rain events when fish actively move upstream.

animals.name: Lake Sturgeon
animals.behavior_notes: Lake Sturgeon congregate in the shallows of Great Lakes tributaries to spawn in late spring when water temperatures reach 55–65°F. They can sometimes be seen rolling or breaking the surface in spawning aggregations.
animals.viewing_tips: The Tahquamenon River and other Upper Peninsula tributaries are among the better spots for observing spawning activity in May. Early morning visits to river mouths and shallow rocky areas give the best odds of sightings.

animals.name: White Sturgeon
parks: Columbia River Gorge National Scenic Area
animals.behavior_notes: White Sturgeon are among the largest freshwater fish in North America and gather in the Columbia River during spring for spawning. They occasionally roll or breach near the surface, giving observers a dramatic view of their prehistoric form.
animals.viewing_tips: Bonneville Dam fish ladders and the adjacent viewing windows provide exceptional looks at White Sturgeon in the Columbia River. The Bonneville Fish Hatchery nearby also maintains large display sturgeon in outdoor ponds.

animals.name: Paddlefish
animals.behavior_notes: Paddlefish congregate in large slow pools of the Current and Jacks Fork Rivers in early spring ahead of spawning, filter-feeding near the surface with their distinctive paddle-shaped rostrums breaking the water. Their prehistoric appearance makes them unmistakable when spotted.
animals.viewing_tips: Look from high riverbanks over large, slow pools in early morning when fish are actively surface feeding. The lower Current River below Akers offers historically reliable sightings, though populations are reduced from historic levels.

animals.name: Alligator Gar
animals.behavior_notes: Alligator Gar are most active and visible in summer when warm river and bayou temperatures drive them to surface-gulp air in shallow backwaters. They often bask just below the surface or roll visibly in calm water during low-oxygen conditions.
animals.viewing_tips: Slow-moving bayous and oxbow lakes within Big Thicket, especially off the Neches River, offer the best sighting opportunities. Scan calm surface waters from elevated banks or a canoe at dawn when gar are most active near shore.

animals.name: Manta Ray
animals.behavior_notes: Oceanic Manta Rays frequent warm Gulf Stream waters off the Florida Keys in summer, often seen filter-feeding near the surface or performing acrobatic breaches. They are drawn to plankton blooms and cleaning stations on shallow reefs.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling or diving at offshore reef sites such as Molasses Reef in the Florida Keys offers the best chance of an encounter during calm summer days. Boat-based spotters can sometimes locate mantas feeding at the surface before snorkelers enter the water.

animals.name: Whale Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Whale sharks aggregate in warm Gulf Stream waters during summer months, often feeding near the surface on fish spawn and plankton blooms. They are slow-moving filter feeders and tend to be docile around divers.
animals.viewing_tips: Book a guided snorkel or dive charter out of Key West or Islamorada that specifically targets whale shark sightings; encounters are opportunistic and best confirmed through local dive operators who track recent sightings.

animals.name: Hammerhead Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Great hammerheads and scalloped hammerheads move into shallow coastal Florida waters during summer, hunting stingrays and fish in seagrass beds and reef edges. They are most active during crepuscular hours near drop-offs.
animals.viewing_tips: Join a dive trip departing from Homestead Bayfront Marina into Biscayne's outer reef zones; early morning dives along reef ledges offer the best chance of a sighting, though encounters are not guaranteed.

animals.name: Great White Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Great white sharks congregate around pinniped colonies at the Channel Islands in fall, taking advantage of juvenile elephant seals and sea lions learning to swim. They often breach or surface during predatory strikes near rocky haul-out sites.
animals.viewing_tips: Take a boat tour from Ventura or Oxnard toward Santa Rosa or San Miguel Island and watch from the deck near seal haul-outs; certified cage dive operators in the broader California coast area improve your odds significantly.

animals.name: Bull Shark
animals.behavior_notes: Bull sharks are uniquely capable of tolerating fresh and brackish water and are known to venture deep into the Everglades river system and Florida Bay. They are highly active hunters at dawn and dusk, patrolling shallow estuarine channels.
animals.viewing_tips: Kayak or boat through the Ten Thousand Islands region of Everglades NP with a guided tour; spotting fins near channel edges at low tide is possible, but sightings remain unpredictable — maintain safe distance at all times.

animals.name: Coelacanth
parks: None — not found in US waters
animals.behavior_notes: The coelacanth is an extremely rare deep-sea fish found primarily off the coasts of South Africa, the Comoros Islands, and Indonesia — it does not inhabit US waters in the wild. It is a living fossil considered functionally extinct in accessible ranges.
animals.viewing_tips: Coelacanths cannot be viewed in the wild within the United States; your best option is to see preserved or live specimens at major aquariums such as the Monterey Bay Aquarium or the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History.

animals.name: Brook Trout
animals.behavior_notes: Brook trout thrive in cold, clear mountain streams and are most active in spring and fall when water temperatures are optimal. During these months they feed aggressively near riffles and pool edges, making them visible in shallow reaches.
animals.viewing_tips: Wade slowly into the headwater streams along Skyline Drive in Shenandoah NP on calm early mornings; look for dart-like movement in sunlit pool shallows, and use polarized sunglasses to cut surface glare for the best visibility.

animals.name: Largemouth Bass
animals.behavior_notes: Largemouth bass move into shallow vegetated areas in spring to spawn, making them highly visible and accessible near lily pads, submerged logs, and shoreline structure. Males actively guard nests in water as shallow as 1–3 feet during this period.
animals.viewing_tips: Paddle a kayak or canoe quietly along the edges of oxbow lakes and backwater sloughs in Big Thicket at first light; bass are easiest to spot in clear, calm water near visible structure — polarized sunglasses are essential.

animals.name: Monarch Butterfly
parks: Point Pelee National Park adjacent areas
animals.behavior_notes: During fall migration, Monarchs congregate in large roosts overnight and actively nectar on milkweed and goldenrod during warm midday hours. They funnel through coastal peninsulas and lakeshores on their journey to Mexican overwintering sites.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit coastal refuges and peninsulas during peak September migration; look for large orange clusters on tree branches at dawn roost sites and watch nectar-rich flower patches during midday warmth.

animals.name: Eastern Tiger Swallowtail
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Tiger Swallowtails are most active on warm, sunny mornings when they visit flowers for nectar and males puddle on moist soil to extract minerals. Multiple broods are produced throughout spring and summer.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan flower gardens, roadsides with wildflowers, and moist streamside gravel bars along park roads; males are especially conspicuous puddling near muddy creek edges in morning hours.

animals.name: Painted Lady Butterfly
animals.behavior_notes: Painted Ladies are highly migratory and irruptive, with population explosions following wet winters that produce abundant thistle. They nectar aggressively on composites and thistles during warm midday periods.
animals.viewing_tips: Look for them on thistle, aster, and cosmos blooms in open meadows and roadsides; migration years produce spectacular numbers so check local reports for irruption events before planning a trip.

animals.name: Luna Moth
animals.behavior_notes: Luna Moths are nocturnal and fly only for about a week as adults since they have no mouths and do not feed. Males use large feathery antennae to detect female pheromones and are attracted to lights on warm, calm nights.
animals.viewing_tips: Check porch lights, white sheets with black lights, and lit windows on warm humid nights near deciduous forests with walnut, birch, or sweetgum trees; look for resting adults on tree trunks at dawn.

animals.name: Cecropia Moth
animals.behavior_notes: North America's largest native moth, the Cecropia flies only at night and does not feed as an adult, living solely to reproduce. Females emit pheromones after midnight that can draw males from miles away.
animals.viewing_tips: Set up a black light and white sheet near forest edges with cherry, maple, or elderberry trees on calm warm nights; finding a freshly emerged female at dusk dramatically increases your chances of attracting males.

animals.name: American Bumble Bee
animals.behavior_notes: American Bumble Bees forage on a wide variety of native prairie wildflowers and are most active in morning hours before peak heat. Queens establish colonies in spring and workers peak in midsummer.
animals.viewing_tips: Focus on native tallgrass prairie remnants and wildflower-rich roadsides with clovers, bergamot, and coneflowers; this species has declined significantly so document sightings on iNaturalist to aid conservation efforts.

animals.name: Firefly (Eastern)
animals.behavior_notes: Eastern Fireflies produce species-specific flash patterns during warm humid evenings to attract mates, with peak activity occurring 30–90 minutes after sunset. Synchronous firefly events at Great Smoky Mountains NP are a spectacular natural phenomenon.
animals.viewing_tips: Find meadows and forest edges near streams on warm, humid, moonless nights in June; the synchronous firefly display at Elkmont in the Smokies requires a ranger-led permit program so book well in advance.

animals.name: Periodical Cicada
animals.behavior_notes: Periodical Cicadas emerge synchronously when soil temperatures reach 64°F, with billions appearing simultaneously in 13- or 17-year cycles. Males sing in deafening choruses from treetops during midday to attract females.
animals.viewing_tips: Check USDA Cicada emergence maps to target active brood years and locations; visit mature deciduous forests with oaks and hickories during emergence years for an extraordinary spectacle of millions of insects.

animals.name: Dragonfly (Common Green Darner)
animals.behavior_notes: Common Green Darners are one of the few migratory dragonflies in North America, forming large southbound swarms along coastlines and ridges during fall. They hunt actively for flying insects on warm mornings before migrating with cold fronts.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit coastal peninsulas, hawk-watch ridges, and wetland edges the day after a cold front passes in September; swarms of hundreds to thousands can be seen flying south along coastal dune lines and open marshes.

animals.name: Praying Mantis
animals.behavior_notes: Praying Mantises reach adult size by late summer and are most visible in August through October when they hunt from tall grasses, goldenrod, and garden plants. Females deposit egg cases on plant stems in fall before dying.
animals.viewing_tips: Walk slowly through tall meadow grasses, goldenrod patches, and garden perennial beds in late summer; look for their distinctive triangular head and cryptic green or brown coloration blending with stems and leaves.

animals.name: Walking Stick
animals.behavior_notes: Walking sticks are most active at dusk and night when they feed on leaves of oak, cherry, and other deciduous trees. During daylight hours they remain motionless on branches, relying on camouflage to avoid predators.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan the undersides of leaves on low shrubs and tree branches at dusk with a red-filtered flashlight. Look for slight movement or irregular twig-like shapes that seem out of place.

animals.name: Tarantula (Desert Blonde)
animals.behavior_notes: Male Desert Blonde tarantulas wander extensively during September and October in search of females during mating season. This annual migration brings them out into the open in large numbers, making fall the prime viewing window.
animals.viewing_tips: Drive slowly along desert roads near Saguaro NP or Joshua Tree at dusk when males cross open ground. Get out and walk dry washes and sandy flats — males can sometimes be spotted every few hundred yards during peak migration.

animals.name: Black Widow Spider
animals.behavior_notes: Black widows are nocturnal hunters that emerge after dark to tend their irregular, tangled webs often built in rock crevices, under ledges, and in dark sheltered spaces. Warmer spring and summer nights increase their activity and web-building behavior.
animals.viewing_tips: Use a UV/blacklight flashlight after dark — black widow silk fluoresces under ultraviolet light, making webs and sometimes the spider itself glow. Check rock overhangs, pit toilet structures, and the undersides of picnic tables. Never reach into dark spaces without looking first.

animals.name: American Horseshoe Crab
parks: Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area
animals.behavior_notes: American horseshoe crabs mass on sandy beaches to spawn during high tides around the new and full moons in May and June. Females crawl ashore at dusk to lay eggs in the sand while smaller males cluster around them, creating dramatic and ancient spectacles on Atlantic beaches.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit Delaware Bay beaches or Cape Hatteras shorelines during high tide on nights near a full or new moon in late May for peak spawning. Walk quietly along the surf line at dusk and look for helmet-shaped shells moving in the shallows — numbers can reach into the thousands on prime nights.

animals.name: Giant Water Bug
animals.behavior_notes: Giant water bugs are aggressive aquatic predators that lurk in slow-moving freshwater ponds, marshes, and streams, ambushing tadpoles, small fish, and insects. Warmer spring months stimulate feeding and mating activity, and males carry fertilized eggs on their backs during this period.
animals.viewing_tips: Shine a flashlight into shallow, still freshwater pools or slow marsh edges at dusk — giant water bugs are attracted to lights and often visible just below the surface. Look for the distinctive flattened oval body up to 4 inches long clinging to submerged vegetation near the Everglades sloughs or Big Thicket creek margins.

animals.name: Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific octopuses are most active during cooler months when water temperatures drop, prompting foraging behavior along rocky intertidal zones. They emerge from dens at dawn and dusk to hunt crabs and mollusks.
animals.viewing_tips: Look in rocky tide pools and kelp-fringed coves at low tide. Bring a flashlight for examining crevices and under ledges where they hide during the day.

animals.name: Giant Pacific Octopus
animals.behavior_notes: Giant Pacific Octopuses den in rocky subtidal areas during winter and are more active nocturnally, venturing out to hunt fish, shrimp, and crab. Winter months align with spawning season when females tend egg masses.
animals.viewing_tips: Best viewed via scuba diving in Puget Sound or the Strait of Juan de Fuca. Shore-based viewing requires very low tides and careful searching of large boulders and cave openings.

animals.name: Bioluminescent Dinoflagellates
animals.behavior_notes: Dinoflagellates bloom in warm, nutrient-rich coastal waters during summer months, producing blue-green bioluminescence when disturbed by waves or movement. Calm, moonless nights in late summer produce the most vivid displays.
animals.viewing_tips: Visit on a new moon night to reduce light pollution and walk into shallow surf or kayak to disturb the water. Avoid areas with artificial lighting as it masks the glow.

animals.name: Jellyfish (Moon)
animals.behavior_notes: Moon jellyfish bloom in coastal bays and harbors during summer when water warms and plankton concentrations peak. They drift passively with currents and often aggregate in large pulsing groups near the surface.
animals.viewing_tips: Scan calm harbor waters, coves, and protected bays from docks or kayaks. Early morning on windless days often reveals large surface aggregations. Avoid touching as they can cause mild skin irritation.

animals.name: Dungeness Crab
animals.behavior_notes: Dungeness crabs migrate into shallower estuarine and sandy-bottom nearshore waters in late fall and winter, congregating in large numbers prior to and during molting season. Males become especially active as they seek mates.
animals.viewing_tips: Wade into shallow sandy-bottomed estuaries at low tide and look carefully under rocks and in eelgrass beds. Glass-bottom kayaks or snorkeling in clear, calm bays can provide excellent views without disturbing them.

animals.name: American Lobster
animals.behavior_notes: American lobsters move into shallower rocky coastal waters during summer when water temperatures warm, making them more accessible to snorkelers and divers. They emerge from rocky crevices at dusk to forage for mussels and urchins.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkel or freedive around rocky ledges and boulder fields in 5–20 feet of water at dusk. Look for their antennae protruding from under ledges. Lobster boats in Acadia's waters also indicate active habitat zones.

animals.name: Coral (Elkhorn)
animals.behavior_notes: Elkhorn coral is a critically endangered species that once dominated shallow Florida reef zones. In summer, spawning events occur a few nights after the full moon when colonies release egg-sperm bundles simultaneously.
animals.viewing_tips: Snorkeling and diving at Biscayne National Park's reef tracts offers the best access. Join a ranger-led snorkel program for guided reef interpretation. Elkhorn is protected — do not touch or stand on coral.

animals.name: Coral (Brain)
animals.behavior_notes: Brain corals are slow-growing, dome-shaped colonies found on shallow and mid-depth reefs. Spring months offer optimal water clarity and calmer seas, allowing excellent observation of the coral's characteristic maze-like surface patterns and resident fish.
animals.viewing_tips: Trunk Bay in Virgin Islands NP offers a marked snorkel trail with interpretive plaques near brain coral formations. Arrive early morning before afternoon winds chop the water surface.

animals.name: Sea Anemone
animals.behavior_notes: Sea anemones are sessile predators that remain attached to intertidal rocks year-round, but spring low tides expose their colorful beds during daylight hours when they are fully extended and actively feeding. Giant green anemones are especially visible in large colonies.
animals.viewing_tips: Check tide tables and visit at extreme low tides (below 0.5 feet) when anemone beds are most exposed. Olympic's tide pools at Rialto Beach and Kalaloch offer spectacular spring displays. Step carefully on dry rocks only.

animals.name: Starfish (Sunflower Sea Star)
animals.behavior_notes: Sunflower sea stars were once the largest and fastest sea stars on the Pacific Coast but have been decimated by Sea Star Wasting Syndrome since 2013 and are now critically endangered. Remaining individuals are most sightable in cooler fall waters at subtidal depths.
animals.viewing_tips: Sightings are extremely rare from shore. Report any confirmed sightings to iNaturalist or local marine monitoring programs. Subtidal scuba diving in northern Washington or Alaska waters offers the best remaining chance of observation.

animals.name: Pacific Sea Nettle
animals.behavior_notes: Pacific Sea Nettles drift with ocean currents in large aggregations during late summer, making them highly visible near the surface. Their long trailing tentacles and golden-brown bells are especially prominent during calm, sunny days when they concentrate in sheltered bays.
animals.viewing_tips: Book a kayak or snorkel tour around Channel Islands or Monterey Bay in late summer for the best chance of encountering large jellyfish blooms. Look from piers or coastal overlooks during calm, flat-sea conditions when jellies rise to the surface.

animals.name: Mantis Shrimp
animals.behavior_notes: Mantis shrimp are most active at dawn and dusk in spring and early summer, emerging from rocky crevices and reef burrows to hunt. Warm shallow waters of Florida's coral reef ecosystems allow them to be spotted more frequently during this season.
animals.viewing_tips: Join a guided snorkel or scuba dive tour in Biscayne National Park's shallow reef areas and scan rocky rubble and coral heads carefully — mantis shrimp are cryptic and stay close to burrows. Bring a dive light even during daylight to illuminate crevices where they hide.
